name: Filming with Light: A Workshop by Luis Macías
description: A hands-on workshop on making cinema without a camera, by creating, manipulating and altering moving images with light on the film emulsion.Facilitated by analog film practitioner Luis Macías (Crater-Lab, Barcelona), the workshop introduces the fundamentals of camera-less 16mm filmmaking: how to create and manipulate moving images directly on celluloid.Working with black-and-white film, you will try three techniques:Rayographs: making abstract images by placing objects directly on film stock and exposing their shadows and textures with flashlights.Flat printing: copying and altering existing negative or positive film through direct emulsion-to-emulsion contact printing, a fast way to overprint, layer materials and build rhythmic fades.Darkroom processing: developing film under safelight to watch and adjust the image in real time through positive development, solarization and chemical manipulation.Suitable for beginners and experienced makers. name: K se Karuna: India’s Intellectual Inheritance
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that asks where our political vocabulary, that we use almost every day - actually came from:Liberty, equality, fraternity. Three words that built the modern nation, and all three arrived here from somewhere else. What if the organising idea had come from within South Asia instead?The nation-making of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries settled on that trio, and we have lived inside it ever since: in constitutional safeguards, in the language of rights, in what we understand democratic life to guarantee. Ideas that germinated in the continental world and travelled into the Global South as imports, carrying both a formal-legal meaning and a substantive promise for how people might live together.Pia David turns to a different inheritance. Karuṇā, compassion, is an idea that emerges from within this geography, and it has its own long history of thinking about difference, diversity and ethical living. Not only in the ancient past, but through the reformist and political thought of modern India, where it kept resurfacing in arguments about what a shared life demands.The question the lecture leaves us with is a live one. What would it mean to treat karuṇā not as sentiment but as political method?A way of addressing global conflict, human despair, and the particular poverty that enters political discourse when compassion goes missing from it?The session explores:How liberty, equality and fraternity became the default grammar of modern political lifeKaruṇā as an idea with its own intellectual lineage in South Asia, ancient and modernHow questions of diversity, difference and ethical living were imagined from within this regionWhat compassion offers as a mode of praxis, not just a normative horizon for theory, but something politics could actually doAbout the SpeakerPia David is from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh, and is trained as a political scientist. As a Foundation for Universal Responsibility Dalai Lama Studies Fellow in 2023, she worked on Dharma and Dhamma: A Modern Reading of Gandhi and Ambedkar in the Context of Deep Diversity. Her interests span liberal political philosophy and social and political thought from South Asia in the context of the world. She can be found on long walks through forested gardens, tombs and ruins, usually with friends, sometimes in solitude, never without music. Her current favourite is Libertango. She lives in Delhi, wondering about Mir's lament on his exile.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

description: About the LectureWhen we picture India's borders, we picture conflict, army men, terrorists. Where are the people who actually live there?For them, negotiating the border is a Tuesday. We meet people who deal with borders in their own particular ways, and who manage to come out of the darkest possibilities with lightness, humour and hope. Along the way: migration, kinship, environment, and identities that refuse to sit still.The invitation is to look past the media's obsession with "Us vs Them", towards something more complicated and more accurate — a world of "Us and Them".The session explores:What daily life actually looks like when a border runs through itMigration, kinship and fluid identity at India's marginsHow humour and hope survive in places we only hear about during conflictWhy "Us vs Them" is a poor description of the borderlands — and what replaces itAbout the SpeakerSamarth Mahajan is a Mumbai-based filmmaker with a particular interest in narratives from India's border areas. His work includes two national award-winning documentaries: Borderlands (2021), which explores lives defined by India's borders, and The Unreserved (2017), which captures stories from the general compartments of Indian Railways. His films have screened across six continents to favourable reviews and received broadcast and theatrical releases in India. IIT Kharagpur has recognised him as a Young Alumni Achiever. His other passion is organising food walks through the crowded streets of Old Delhi, South Mumbai and Amritsar, and he is currently wrapping his debut fiction short.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Who Does the City Belong To?
description: Who Does the City Belong To?A conversation on public space and the lawYou have probably stood in front of a barricade this year. A road closed with no notice. A park gate locked at night. A station shut, a lane that used to be a shortcut now ending in a guard and a boom. Most of us have learned to route around it without thinking.But there’s a question underneath that almost none of us can answer: what are we actually entitled to in a public space and what happens when that space is closed, fenced or policed?In this edition of The Human City Conversations, we’ll ask what the Constitution actually gives us by way of a right to assemble and to protest. Whether a government can simply take a Jantar Mantar away. Whether there is such a thing as a right to walk in an Indian city, and who in Delhi really has it. And how much of what we call planning is in truth a question of who is expected to justify their presence in public, and who is not.It isn’t a lecture, and it isn’t a complaint session. It’s an hour of conversation, in plain words, followed by your questions put directly to someone who has spent two decades arguing these things in court.About the guestMihira Sood is a lawyer and scholar in the field of women’s rights, and practices at the Supreme Court of India and the Delhi High Court. She has taught at Jindal Global Law School and National Law University Delhi, and holds degrees from NALSAR University of Law, Hyderabad, and Columbia Law School, New York. She was among the youngest members to assist the Justice Verma Committee, whose recommendations reshaped India’s criminal law on sexual violence. She writes and speaks widely on women’s rights, feminist jurisprudence, equality law and civil liberties, and is a regular commentator in the national press. She has recently written a book Courting Equality which focusses on the Landmark Cases in the Battle for Women’s Rights (Juggernaut) traces fifty years of the law’s encounter with women’s lives — from the anti-dowry agitations of the 1970s, through Shah Bano and the Uniform Civil Code debate, to the Nirbhaya movement and its continuing reverberations, and on to the present backlash against the supposed misuse of these very laws.Copies will be on sale at Kunzum on the evening, at 20% off.About the seriesThe Human City Conversations is the live edition of The Human City Podcast, hosted by Ruchita Bansal, which for the past year has asked how Indian cities are planned, built and experienced — and who they are built for. name: The Criminal Profiling Masterclass
description: Inside a Profiler's Mind: Four Sessions on Criminal ProfilingThink like a profiler. Reason like a scientist.You've probably watched the shows. The detective looks at a crime scene for a few seconds, pauses, and describes the killer right down to his childhood. It's great TV, but is it how profiling actually works?Across four sessions, criminologist and forensic psychologist Rithin Joseph separates movie myth from method. We go from 19th-century attempts to spot criminals by the shape of their skulls, to the FBI's Behavioral Science Unit, to the maths of where offenders live, to how profiling is actually done in 2026. Every session digs into real true crime cases, runs its own hands-on simulation, and has much more along the way, so you won't just be listening. You'll be profiling.Each session stands on its own, so come to one or come to all four. Book all four and get a discount, for anyone who wants the full case file.21st November, 4-6 PM: Can You Tell If I'm a Serial Killer?Profiling's real history is messier than the legend, and much more interesting. We start with Lombroso and phrenology, who believed you could read criminality in someone's face, and look at why those ideas caught on and why they fell apart. Then we follow Hans Gross's turn toward evidence, James Brussel's famous (and contested) Mad Bomber profile, and the rise of the FBI's behavioural analysts. Along the way we ask what profiling can actually tell an investigator, and what it never can.22nd November, 4-6 PM: Same Crime, Different Profiles: Who Gets It Right?Two profilers look at the same crime scene and come back with two different suspects. How does that happen? This session gets into the reasoning behind profiling: patterns drawn from many offenders versus clues taken from one case, and the FBI's famous split between "organised" and "disorganised" offenders, with cases like BTK and Jeffrey Dahmer as reference points. We'll look at where that split helps and where it falls apart, and at the biases that slip in without anyone noticing. Then we'll test ourselves on a fictional scene that has two competing profiles.28th November, 3–5 PM: Where Do Killers Live? The Geography of CrimeA series of crimes leaves more than physical evidence. It leaves a map. Using David Canter's investigative psychology and Kim Rossmo's geographic profiling, we'll look at how offenders move through a city: comfort zones, anchor points, and why distance matters. The DC Sniper case runs through the session. Then we'll take a fictional cluster of crime locations and try to narrow the search ourselves. A warning in advance: these maps deal in probabilities, not GPS coordinates.29th November, 3–5 PM: What Criminal Profiling Looks Like in 2026Instead of asking "what kind of person would do this?", modern profiling asks "what does the evidence actually show?" This session introduces Behavioral Evidence Analysis, which reads the crime scene, the victim's circumstances and the sequence of events before it reaches for any stereotype. We'll work out the difference between how a crime was committed and what it might reveal about the person behind it. Then we'll read a fictional case file twice and watch our conclusions change as new evidence comes in.All sessions at the Gully Labs store, Panchsheel Park.About the speakerRithin Joseph is an Assistant Professor at the School of Behavioural Forensics, National Forensic Sciences University, Delhi, where he teaches criminology and forensic psychology. He is certified in investigative tools including the polygraph, BEOS brain profiling, Layered Voice Analysis and EyeDetect. He is Co-Investigator on an ICSSR-funded study predicting recidivism among first-time offenders, co-author of Crime as the Cause of Criminality and BRICS: Unravelling the Abyss, and a gold medallist in his Master's in Criminology.Four sessions, four case files, and you'll never watch a crime show the same way again.
